decks.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current — Part 1: Magnetic fields from magnets and currents
goals: Draw field-line patterns around a bar magnet and state the properties of magnetic field lines
Apply the right-hand thumb rule to find the field direction around a straight wire and a circular loop
Describe the field inside a solenoid and how it is used to make an electromagnet

slides.heading: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the **magnetic field** of a bar magnet, and the surprising discovery that an **electric current makes a magnetic field** too.
slides.narration: Namaste! A compass needle always points north, a fridge magnet clings to the door, and a scrapyard crane lifts a whole car with a magnet you can switch off. The last one is the clue: electricity and magnetism are closely linked. In this part we map magnetic fields with field lines, and see how wires, loops and coils carrying current become magnets.

slides.heading: Magnets, compasses and magnetic fields
slides.body_md: A **compass needle** is a small bar magnet; its north-seeking end is its **north pole**. The region around a magnet in which its force can be detected is its **magnetic field**. A field has both **strength and direction**.

rows: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
A freely suspended magnet points north–south
The field direction at a point is the way a compass N pole points there
Compass placed near a bar magnet

visual.alt: Table: like poles repel and unlike poles attract; a freely suspended magnet points north and south, as a compass needle does; the field direction at a point is where a compass north pole points

slides.narration: A compass needle is simply a tiny, light magnet free to turn. Its north pole points towards the Earth’s geographic north. Bring it near a bar magnet and it turns, because it is inside that magnet’s field. We define the direction of the field at any point as the direction in which the north pole of a compass needle points there.

slides.heading: Field lines around a bar magnet
slides.body_md: Iron filings or a small compass trace **field lines**: they leave the **N pole**, curve round and enter the **S pole**.

visual.alt: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet. The lines come out of the north pole, curve round through the space outside and enter the south pole. They are crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest, spread out further away, and never cross one another.
visual.caption: Field lines are traced here from a model of the magnet’s two poles. They leave the N pole and enter the S pole, and they never cross.

slides.narration: Sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper over a bar magnet and tap it gently. The filings line up in curves from one pole to the other. You can also trace a curve dot by dot by moving a small compass along. These curves are field lines. Outside the magnet they run from north to south, and they bunch together near the poles, where the field is strongest.

slides.heading: Properties of magnetic field lines

rows: They come out of the **N pole** and go into the **S pole** outside the magnet; inside, they run from S to N
The **tangent** at any point gives the field direction
A compass needle sets along the tangent
Lines are **crowded** where the field is strong
The field is strongest near the poles
At a crossing, a compass would point two ways at once — impossible

visual.alt: Table of properties of magnetic field lines: they leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet and run from south to north inside, forming closed curves; the tangent gives the field direction; crowded lines mean a strong field, strongest near the poles; and no two lines cross, because a compass cannot point two ways at once

slides.narration: Four rules describe every field-line drawing. Lines go from north to south outside the magnet and continue from south to north inside, so each one is a closed loop. The tangent gives the direction. Crowding shows strength. And lines never cross, because at a crossing point a compass would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.

slides.heading: Quick check: crossing lines
slides.body_md: Why can two magnetic field lines never cross each other?
slides.narration: Imagine placing a compass at the crossing point. Which way would its needle point?

slides.heading: A current makes a magnetic field
slides.body_md: In 1820 **Hans Christian Oersted** noticed that a compass needle near a wire **deflects when current flows**. Reversing the current reverses the deflection.

slides.narration: Oersted noticed something remarkable during a lecture: a compass needle near a wire jumped when he switched on the current. A current, he realised, produces a magnetic field around it. When the current is reversed, the needle swings the other way, so the field reverses too. This one observation joined electricity and magnetism, and later led to motors, generators and radio.

slides.body_md: The field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire. Use the **right-hand thumb rule**: thumb along the current, curled fingers show the field.

slides.narration: Pass a thick wire vertically through a sheet of cardboard, sprinkle iron filings, and switch on a large current. The filings form circles around the wire. To find the direction, grip the wire in your right hand with the thumb pointing along the current. Your curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. Here the current flows up, so the field runs anticlockwise when seen from above.

slides.heading: How strong is the field of a straight wire?

headers: Effect on the field at a point
rows: Field becomes **weaker**: circles get farther apart

visual.alt: Table: increasing the current makes the field stronger; moving farther from the wire makes it weaker, with circles farther apart; reversing the current reverses the field

slides.narration: Two things decide how strong the field is at a point near a straight wire. More current gives a stronger field. And the field fades as you move away, which is why the circles drawn further out are spaced more widely. A compass placed close to a wire carrying a large current swings sharply; the same compass a metre away hardly moves.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: using the right-hand thumb rule
slides.body_md: Current flows **vertically upwards** in a wire. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point due **east** of the wire?
bullets: Step 1 — point the right thumb **upwards**, along the current.
Step 2 — the fingers curl **anticlockwise** as seen from above.
Step 3 — going anticlockwise round a circle (seen from above), the point on the **east** side moves towards the **north**.
Answer — the field at the east point is directed **north**.
Check — at the west point it would be south: opposite sides of a circle have opposite directions.

visual.alt: Table for an upward current: east of the wire the field points north, north of the wire it points west, west of the wire south, and south of the wire east

slides.narration: Use your own right hand as you listen. Thumb up. Look down at your curled fingers from above: they go anticlockwise. Now imagine walking anticlockwise around the wire. On the east side you are heading north. That is the field direction there. Doing this with a real hand, not in your head, avoids most mistakes.

slides.heading: Quick check: a vertical wire
slides.body_md: Current flows vertically downwards in a wire. Seen from above, how do the magnetic field lines run?
slides.narration: Point your right thumb downwards, then look at your fingers from above.

slides.heading: Field of a circular loop
slides.body_md: Each small part of the loop acts like a straight wire. Near the wire the lines are circles; at the **centre** they are **nearly straight** and all point the **same way**.

visual.alt: Magnetic field of a circular current loop, seen from the side, cut through its centre. Where the wire comes out of the page at the top and goes into the page at the bottom, the field lines are circles around the wire. Near the centre of the loop the lines are nearly straight and all point the same way.
visual.caption: Section through the centre of the loop: ⊙ current out of the page, ⊗ current into the page.

slides.narration: Bend the straight wire into a circle. Near each part of the wire the lines are still small circles. But inside the loop, the contributions from every part of the wire point in the same direction, so they add up. At the centre the lines become almost straight. A loop is like a very thin, flat magnet.

slides.heading: Making the loop’s field stronger
slides.body_md: At the centre of a coil, the field increases with the **current** and with the **number of turns** $n$: the fields of the turns add up.

visual.alt: Table for coils of the same radius: one turn carrying I gives field B; ten turns carrying I give 10B; ten turns carrying 2I give 20B

slides.narration: If one turn gives a certain field at the centre, ten turns wound together carry the same current round ten times, so the field is ten times as strong. Doubling the current doubles it again. That is why practical electromagnets use many turns of thin insulated copper wire.

slides.heading: The solenoid
slides.body_md: A **solenoid** is a long coil of many turns. Its field is like that of a **bar magnet**, and **inside it the field is uniform**: parallel, equally spaced lines.

visual.alt: A current-carrying solenoid cut along its length. Current comes out of the page along the top row of turns and goes into the page along the bottom row. Inside, the field lines are parallel straight lines, showing a uniform field; outside they curve round like those of a bar magnet, with the north pole at the end where the lines come out.
visual.caption: ⊙ current out of the page, ⊗ current into the page. The lines are traced from the field of all the turns together.

slides.narration: Wind many loops close together into a long cylinder and you get a solenoid. Outside, its field looks just like a bar magnet’s, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. Inside, the lines are straight, parallel and evenly spaced. That means the field is the same everywhere inside: a uniform field.

slides.heading: Which end is north?
slides.body_md: Curl the fingers of your **right hand** in the direction of the current in the turns; the **thumb points to the N pole** of the solenoid.

headers: Seen from one end, current flows…

visual.alt: Table: if the current seen from one end of a solenoid flows anticlockwise, that end is a north pole; if it flows clockwise, that end is a south pole

slides.narration: This is the same right-hand rule used another way. For a coil, curl your fingers along the current in the turns, and your thumb points along the field inside, towards the north pole. An easy check: look at one end. If the current there goes anticlockwise, you are looking at a north pole; clockwise means a south pole.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: polarity of a solenoid
slides.body_md: Rina looks at the right-hand end of a solenoid and sees the current going **clockwise**. What poles are at its two ends, and which way does the field point inside?
bullets: Step 1 — clockwise current seen from an end means that end is a **south pole**: the right end is **S**.
Step 2 — so the left end is **N**.
Step 3 — inside a solenoid the field runs from S to N, so inside it points **from right to left**.
Check — right hand: fingers along the current, thumb points left, towards N. Consistent.

visual.alt: Table: the right end, with clockwise current, is a south pole; the left end, where the same current looks anticlockwise, is a north pole

slides.narration: Notice that the same current looks clockwise from one end and anticlockwise from the other, so the two ends must have opposite poles. Inside the solenoid, field lines go from the south end to the north end, just as inside a bar magnet. Always finish with a quick right-hand check.

slides.heading: The electromagnet
slides.body_md: Placing a **soft iron core** inside a solenoid makes a strong **electromagnet**. It is a magnet only while current flows.

slides.narration: Put a rod of soft iron inside the solenoid and switch on. The iron becomes strongly magnetised and the electromagnet can lift heavy loads. Switch off, and soft iron loses its magnetism almost at once, so the load drops. This on–off control is what makes electromagnets so useful in cranes, electric bells, relays and loudspeakers.

slides.heading: Electromagnet or permanent magnet?

rows: Can be changed: more turns or current

visual.alt: Comparison table: an electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows, its strength can be changed with turns or current and its polarity reversed with the current, and it uses a soft iron core; a permanent magnet is always magnetic with fixed strength and polarity, made of steel or special alloys

slides.narration: An electromagnet can be switched on and off, made stronger or weaker, and have its poles swapped, all by controlling the current. A permanent magnet cannot do any of that, but needs no power. Steel keeps its magnetism, which suits permanent magnets; soft iron loses it easily, which suits electromagnets.

slides.heading: Quick check: a stronger electromagnet
slides.body_md: Which change will make an electromagnet stronger?
slides.narration: Think about what adds up inside the coil, and what the soft iron core does.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Field lines: N to S outside, closed curves, crowded where strong, never cross.
A current produces a magnetic field (Oersted).
Straight wire: concentric circles; right-hand thumb rule; stronger with more current, weaker further away.
Loop: nearly straight lines at the centre; field grows with current and number of turns.
Solenoid: like a bar magnet, uniform field inside; with a soft iron core it is an electromagnet.

rows: Thumb along current, fingers curl with field
Circles near the wire, nearly straight at the centre
Same rule for each part of the loop
Like a bar magnet; uniform inside
Fingers along current, thumb to N

visual.alt: Summary table: a straight wire gives concentric circles, found with the right-hand thumb rule; a loop gives circles near the wire and nearly straight lines at the centre; a solenoid gives a bar-magnet field, uniform inside, with the thumb pointing to its north pole when the fingers follow the current

slides.narration: Here is Part 1 in one table. Learn the three field shapes and the one right-hand rule that gives every direction. And remember the two ways to strengthen the field of a coil: more current and more turns, plus a soft iron core to turn it into a powerful electromagnet.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Field-line diagrams: arrows from **N to S outside**, lines **closed**, **never crossing**, denser near the poles.
Use the **right hand** for fields of currents (thumb rule); the left hand is only for force (Part 2).
For a straight wire, draw **circles with arrows**; mention that the field gets **weaker with distance**.
Solenoid answers: "**uniform** field inside", "like a **bar magnet** outside".
Electromagnet: name the **soft iron** core and the two ways to increase strength (**turns**, **current**).
slides.narration: Diagram marks are lost for missing arrows, crossing lines and open curves, so be careful with your field-line sketches. Many students use the wrong hand: for the field around a current, it is always the right hand. And when asked about a solenoid, the key words examiners look for are uniform field inside and bar magnet outside.

decks.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current — Part 2: Force on a conductor, AC and DC, and domestic circuits
goals: Use Fleming’s left-hand rule to predict the direction of force on a conductor
Distinguish DC and AC, state the frequency of AC in India and give advantages of AC
Explain live, neutral and earth wires, fuses, overloading and short-circuiting

slides.heading: Forces, AC and safe wiring
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a magnet **pushes** on a wire carrying current; the two kinds of current, **DC and AC**; and how the wiring in our homes is made **safe**.
slides.narration: A current makes a magnetic field. So, just as two magnets push and pull each other, a magnet should push on a wire carrying current. It does, and that push spins every electric fan and motor. In this part we predict the direction of that force, compare the current from a cell with the current from the mains, and look inside the wiring of a house.

slides.heading: A magnet pushes a current-carrying rod
slides.body_md: A light aluminium rod between the poles of a magnet is **displaced sideways** when current flows. The force is **perpendicular to both** the current and the field.

slides.narration: Hang a light aluminium rod between the poles of a strong horseshoe magnet, and connect it to a cell through a key. Close the key and the rod jumps sideways. It moves neither along the field nor along the current, but at right angles to both. André-Marie Ampère suggested that the magnet and the conductor push on each other with equal and opposite forces.

slides.heading: What controls the force?

rows: Force reverses: rod moves the other way

visual.alt: Table: reversing either the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged; the force is largest when the rod is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel

slides.narration: Try each change in turn. Reverse the current, and the rod jumps the other way. Swap the magnet’s poles, and the same happens. Reverse both, and the two reversals cancel. The force is biggest when the rod is at right angles to the field, and disappears completely when the rod lies along the field lines.

slides.body_md: Stretch the **first finger**, **second finger** and **thumb** of the **left hand** mutually perpendicular. First finger → **field**, second finger → **current**: the thumb gives the **force (motion)**.

slides.narration: Hold your left hand so that the thumb, first finger and second finger are all at right angles to one another. Point the first finger along the field, from north to south. Point the second finger along the current. Your thumb now points in the direction of the force, which is the way the conductor moves. A memory aid: First for Field, seCond for Current, thuMb for Motion.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: applying the left-hand rule
slides.body_md: In the set-up on the earlier slide, the field points **downwards** (N pole above) and the current in the rod flows **towards you**. Which way is the rod pushed?
bullets: Step 1 — left hand: first finger pointing **down** (field).
Step 2 — turn the hand so the second finger points **towards you** (current).
Step 3 — the thumb now points to **your right**.
Answer — the rod is pushed **to the right**, as the diagram shows.
Check — reverse the current (away from you) and the thumb points left.

visual.alt: Table: field down and current towards you gives force to the right; field down and current away gives force to the left; field up and current towards you gives force to the left

slides.narration: Do this with your actual left hand. First finger down for the field. Now rotate your wrist until your second finger points at your own chest, along the current. Your thumb points to the right. That matches the rod moving right in the diagram. If either the field or the current is reversed, the thumb swings to the left.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a beam of electrons
slides.body_md: A beam of **electrons** moves towards the **east** through a magnetic field that points **vertically downwards**. In which direction is the beam deflected?
bullets: Step 1 — electrons are negative, so the **current** is opposite to their motion: towards the **west**.
Step 2 — left hand: first finger **down** (field), second finger **west** (current).
Step 3 — the thumb points **south**.
Answer — the beam is deflected towards the **south**.
Check — positive particles moving east would be pushed north: the opposite way.

visual.alt: Table: electrons moving east in a downward field are a westward current and are pushed south; positive charges moving east are an eastward current and are pushed north

slides.narration: The trap here is the electron. The rule uses conventional current, which flows opposite to the electrons. So first turn the electron motion into a current direction, west. Then apply the left-hand rule as usual. If the question had been about protons or other positive particles moving east, the current would be east and the force north.

slides.heading: Quick check: reversing both
slides.body_md: If both the current in a rod and the magnetic field are reversed, what happens to the force on the rod?
slides.narration: Each reversal on its own turns the force round. What do two reversals do together?

slides.heading: Where this force is used

rows: Electric motor (fans, mixers, pumps, washing machines)
Turns a coil in a magnetic field
Pushes a coil attached to the cone back and forth
Electric meters with a moving coil

visual.alt: Table: in electric motors in fans, mixers, pumps and washing machines the force turns a coil; in a loudspeaker it moves a coil attached to the cone; in moving-coil meters it turns a pointer

slides.narration: This small sideways push is one of the most useful forces in technology. In a motor, the forces on the two sides of a coil act in opposite directions and make it spin. In a loudspeaker, a coil fixed to the paper cone is pushed back and forth by the changing current, and the cone makes sound. Every ceiling fan in India runs on this idea.

slides.heading: Direct current and alternating current
slides.body_md: **Direct current (DC)** always flows in one direction, as from a cell. **Alternating current (AC)** **reverses its direction periodically**, as from the mains.

visual.alt: Graph of current against time over 40 milliseconds: direct current is a flat line at a constant positive value; alternating current is a sine wave that rises, falls through zero and becomes negative, completing one cycle every 20 milliseconds, so it reverses direction every 10 milliseconds.
visual.caption: In India the mains supply is AC of frequency 50 Hz: one cycle every 20 ms.

slides.narration: A cell pushes charge one way only, so its current is direct current. The mains supply is different: the current flows one way, slows, stops, and then flows the other way, again and again. That is alternating current. On the graph, DC is a flat line, while AC swings above and below zero in a regular wave.

slides.heading: AC in India: 50 hertz
slides.body_md: Mains AC in India has a **frequency of 50 Hz**: 50 complete cycles each second. One cycle takes $\dfrac{1}{50}$ s $= 20$ ms, and the current **changes direction every** $\dfrac{1}{100}$ s.

rows: Can be sent over long distances with much less loss

visual.alt: Comparison table: DC flows one way from cells, batteries and solar panels; AC reverses periodically, comes from power stations, is supplied at 220 volts and 50 hertz in India, and can be transmitted over long distances with much less energy loss

slides.narration: Fifty hertz means fifty complete back-and-forth cycles every second. Since each cycle includes two reversals, the current changes direction a hundred times each second, once every hundredth of a second. The big advantage of AC is that it can be stepped up to very high voltages for transmission, so it travels long distances from power stations with much less energy lost.

slides.heading: Quick check: reversals per second
slides.body_md: How many times does the direction of the 50 Hz mains current reverse in one second?
slides.narration: Count the reversals in a single cycle, then multiply by the number of cycles each second.

slides.heading: Live, neutral and earth
slides.body_md: The potential difference between **live** and **neutral** is **220 V**. Switches and fuses are put in the **live** wire.

rows: At a high potential; carries current to the appliance
Return path; at about zero potential
Safety wire joined to a metal plate deep in the ground

visual.alt: Table of the three wires: live, with red insulation, at high potential, carrying current to the appliance; neutral, black, the return path at about zero potential; earth, green, a safety wire joined to a metal plate buried in the ground

slides.narration: Indian house wiring uses colour codes. The live wire, with red insulation, is at a high potential. The neutral wire, in black, is the return path and stays at about zero potential. Between them is two hundred and twenty volts. The green earth wire is for safety. Switches and fuses always go in the live wire, so that switching off really cuts the appliance off from the high voltage.

slides.heading: Why earthing saves lives
slides.body_md: The **earth wire** joins the **metal body** of an appliance to the ground through a **low-resistance** path. If a live wire touches the body, the current flows to earth, the body stays at **earth potential**, and the user does not get a severe shock.

nodes.label: Fault: live wire touches the metal body
Large current flows through the earth wire
Body stays at earth potential: little or no shock

visual.alt: Flow chart: if a live wire touches the metal body, a large current flows through the earth wire, so the body stays at earth potential and the user is safe, and the large current also blows the fuse

slides.narration: Imagine the insulation inside a washing machine wears through and the live wire touches the metal body. Without an earth wire, anyone touching the machine becomes the path to the ground and gets a dangerous shock. With the earth wire, the current takes the easy, low-resistance path to the ground instead. That surge usually blows the fuse too, cutting off the supply.

slides.heading: Short-circuiting and overloading

rows: Live and neutral wires come into **direct contact**
Too much current is drawn from a circuit
Damaged insulation or a fault in an appliance
Too many appliances on one socket; a sudden rise in supply voltage
Resistance becomes tiny; current rises abruptly

visual.alt: Comparison table: short-circuiting happens when live and neutral touch directly, through damaged insulation or a fault, making the resistance tiny and the current rise abruptly; overloading happens when too much current is drawn, from too many appliances on one socket or a voltage surge, making the wires overheat; in both, a fuse or MCB protects the circuit

slides.narration: Two kinds of fault cause most electrical fires. In a short circuit, live and neutral touch directly, the resistance becomes almost zero, and the current shoots up. In overloading, too many appliances are plugged into one circuit, or the supply voltage jumps, and the total current is too large. In both cases the wires overheat. A fuse, or a miniature circuit breaker, cuts the supply before a fire starts.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: is the circuit overloaded?
slides.body_md: A **5 A** lighting circuit at **220 V** has two 60 W bulbs and a 75 W fan switched on. Can a **1000 W** room heater be plugged into the same circuit?
bullets: Step 1 — load already on: $2 \times 60 + 75 = 195$ W, so $I = \dfrac{195}{220} \approx 0.89$ A.
Step 2 — with the heater: $P = 195 + 1000 = 1195$ W, so $I = \dfrac{1195}{220} \approx 5.4$ A.
Step 3 — 5.4 A is more than the 5 A rating: the circuit would be **overloaded** and the fuse would melt.
Answer — no; the heater should be used on the **15 A** power circuit.

visual.alt: Table: two bulbs and a fan, 195 watts, draw about 0.89 ampere; adding a 1000 watt heater makes 1195 watts and about 5.4 amperes, more than the 5 ampere rating

slides.narration: Appliances in parallel add up: total power is the sum, and total current is that power divided by the voltage. The lights and fan together draw less than one ampere. Add the heater and the current jumps to about five and a half amperes, over the fuse’s limit. That is exactly why heavy appliances have their own fifteen ampere circuit.

slides.heading: Quick check: the earth wire
slides.body_md: Why is the metal body of an electric iron connected to the earth wire?
slides.narration: Think about what would happen if the live wire touched the iron’s metal body while someone was holding it.

slides.heading: Safety devices at a glance

rows: Low-melting wire in series in the live wire melts
Switches off automatically; can be reset
Electric shock from a faulty metal-bodied appliance

visual.alt: Table of safety devices: a fuse and a miniature circuit breaker protect against short circuits and overloading, the fuse by melting and the MCB by switching off and being reset; the earth wire protects against shocks from faulty metal-bodied appliances by giving a low-resistance path to the ground

slides.narration: Modern homes use miniature circuit breakers, which switch off automatically when the current is too large and can simply be switched on again once the fault is fixed. They do the same job as fuses. The earth wire is different: it protects people, not wires. A safe home needs both kinds of protection, and appliances with metal bodies should always use three-pin plugs.

slides.heading: Beyond the board paper: motors and generators
slides.body_md: *Assessed only in school (formative) work, not in the board theory paper.* A **motor** uses the force on a current-carrying coil to turn it. **Electromagnetic induction**: a **changing** magnetic field in a coil produces a current; a **generator** uses this to change mechanical energy into electrical energy.

bullets: Left-hand rule uses **conventional current**: for electrons, reverse the direction first.

sections.heading: 1. Magnetic field and field lines

key_terms.definition_md: The region around a magnet in which its magnetic force can be detected.
The path along which a free north pole would tend to move; its tangent gives the field direction.

visual.alt: Magnetic field lines around a bar magnet. The lines come out of the north pole, curve round through the space outside and enter the south pole. They are crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest, spread out further away, and never cross one another.

rows: They come out of the **N pole** and go into the **S pole** outside the magnet; inside, they run from S to N
The **tangent** at any point gives the field direction
A compass needle sets along the tangent

visuals.alt: Table of properties of magnetic field lines: they leave the north pole and enter the south pole outside the magnet and run from south to north inside, forming closed curves; the tangent gives the field direction; crowded lines mean a strong field, strongest near the poles; and no two lines cross, because a compass cannot point two ways at once

sections.heading: 2. Magnetic field of a current: straight wire, loop and solenoid
sections.body_md:
**Oersted (1820):** a compass needle near a wire is deflected when current flows; reversing the current reverses the deflection. A current produces a magnetic field.

**Straight wire:** field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it. The field is **stronger for a larger current** and **weaker further from the wire**. **Right-hand thumb rule:** grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current; the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines.

**Circular loop:** near the wire the lines are circles; at the **centre** they are **nearly straight**, perpendicular to the plane of the loop, because every part of the loop contributes in the same direction. The field at the centre increases with the **current** and with the **number of turns** (the fields of the turns add up).

**Solenoid:** a coil of many closely wound turns in the shape of a cylinder. Its field is like that of a **bar magnet**, and **inside it is uniform** (parallel straight lines). With the right hand, fingers curled along the current, the thumb points to the **N pole**; equivalently, current anticlockwise as seen from an end makes that end **N**, clockwise makes it **S**.

**Electromagnet:** a solenoid with a **soft iron core**. It is a magnet only while current flows; it is made stronger by **more turns**, **more current** and a suitable core; its polarity reverses with the current. Soft iron loses its magnetism quickly when switched off; steel keeps it (permanent magnets).

key_terms.definition_md: Thumb along the current, curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field.
A long coil of many circular turns of insulated wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder.
A solenoid with a soft iron core, magnetised only while current flows.

sections.heading: 3. Force on a current-carrying conductor
sections.body_md:
A conductor carrying current in a magnetic field experiences a **force** (suggested by Ampère: the magnet and the conductor exert equal and opposite forces on each other). The force is **perpendicular to both** the current and the field.

- Reversing the **current** or the **field** reverses the force; reversing **both** leaves it unchanged.
- The force is **largest** when the current is **perpendicular** to the field and **zero** when it is **parallel**.
- It increases with the current and with the strength of the field.

**Fleming’s left-hand rule:** stretch the thumb, first finger and second finger of the **left hand** mutually perpendicular. **First finger → field**, **second finger → current**, **thumb → force (motion)**. For moving electrons, the current is opposite to their motion.

**Uses:** electric motors (fans, mixers, pumps), loudspeakers, moving-coil meters.

key_terms.definition_md: First finger field, second finger current, thumb motion, on the left hand held mutually perpendicular.

sections.heading: 4. Direct current and alternating current
sections.body_md:
**Direct current (DC)** flows in **one direction** only (cells, batteries, solar panels). **Alternating current (AC)** **reverses direction periodically** (power stations, mains).

In India the mains supply is **AC at 220 V and 50 Hz**: 50 cycles per second, period $\dfrac{1}{50}$ s $= 20$ ms; the current reverses **100 times each second**, i.e. every $\dfrac{1}{100}$ s.

**Advantage of AC:** it can be **transmitted over long distances without much loss of energy** (its voltage is easily stepped up and down).

key_terms.definition_md: Current that flows in one direction only.
Current that reverses its direction periodically; 50 Hz in India.

sections.heading: 5. Domestic electric circuits and safety
sections.body_md:
Mains power reaches a house through **live** (red insulation, high potential) and **neutral** (black, about zero potential) wires; the potential difference between them is **220 V**. It passes through the **main fuse** and the **electricity meter** to a **distribution box**, which feeds separate circuits with their own fuses: a **15 A power circuit** for high-power appliances (geyser, heater, air conditioner) and a **5 A lighting circuit** (bulbs, fans). Appliances are connected **in parallel**, each with a **switch in the live wire**.

**Earth wire** (green) — joined to a metal plate deep in the ground and to the **metal bodies** of appliances. If the live wire touches the body, the earth wire gives a **low-resistance path**, the body stays at **earth potential**, and the user does not get a severe shock; the large current also blows the fuse.

**Short-circuiting** — the live and neutral wires come into **direct contact** (damaged insulation, a fault in an appliance); the current rises abruptly.
**Overloading** — **too much current** is drawn: too many appliances on one socket, or an accidental rise in supply voltage.
**Protection:** the **fuse** (low melting point, in series in the live wire) melts; a **miniature circuit breaker (MCB)** switches off and can be reset. The fuse protects wiring and appliances; earthing protects people.

key_terms.definition_md: Connecting the metal body of an appliance to the ground through a low-resistance wire for safety.
Direct contact between live and neutral wires, causing a sudden large current.
Drawing more current from a circuit than it is designed to carry.

sections.heading: 6. Motor, electromagnetic induction and generator (formative assessment only)
sections.body_md:
*Taught for projects and internal (formative) assessment; not assessed in the 2026-27 board theory paper.*

**Electric motor:** converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. A coil in a magnetic field experiences forces in opposite directions on its two sides and rotates; **split rings (commutator)** reverse the current in the coil every half rotation so that it keeps turning the same way.

**Electromagnetic induction:** a current is induced in a coil when the **magnetic field linked with it changes** — for example while a magnet is moved into or out of the coil; no current flows while the magnet is still.

**Electric generator:** uses electromagnetic induction to convert **mechanical energy into electrical energy**; power-station generators produce AC.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Field-line diagrams without arrows, with crossing lines, or with arrows from S to N outside the magnet.
- Using the left hand for the field of a current (use the **right-hand thumb rule**) or the right hand for the force (use **Fleming’s left-hand rule**).
- Forgetting that the left-hand rule uses **conventional current** — reverse the direction for electrons.
- Saying the force is largest when the wire is along the field (it is **zero** then).
- Writing 50 reversals per second for 50 Hz AC (it is **100**).
- Calling the neutral wire "the earth wire", or putting switches and fuses in the neutral wire.
- Saying a fuse protects people from shocks (that is the **earth wire**; the fuse protects the circuit).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Field-line diagrams: correct shape (1) + arrows and labels (1).
- Rule questions: statement of the rule (1) + correct application with direction (1).
- Domestic-circuit answers: key phrases — "low-resistance path", "earth potential", "live and neutral in direct contact", "low melting point, in series".
- Case-based questions: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice.
- Motor, induction and generator: formative only in 2026-27.

cards.front_md: How is the direction of a magnetic field at a point defined?
cards.back_md: The direction in which the **north pole of a compass needle** points there.

cards.front_md: Direction of field lines outside and inside a bar magnet
cards.back_md: Outside **N → S**; inside **S → N**: closed curves.

cards.front_md: What does crowding of field lines show?
cards.back_md: A **stronger** field (near the poles).

cards.front_md: Why can field lines never cross?
cards.back_md: A compass at the crossing would point **two ways at once** — impossible.

cards.front_md: What did Oersted discover?
cards.back_md: A **current produces a magnetic field**: a compass near a wire deflects when current flows.

cards.front_md: Field lines around a straight current-carrying wire
cards.back_md: **Concentric circles** centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it.

cards.front_md: Right-hand thumb rule
cards.back_md: Thumb along the **current**; curled fingers give the **field** direction.

cards.front_md: Current flows upwards in a vertical wire. Field seen from above?
cards.back_md: **Anticlockwise** circles.

cards.front_md: How does the field of a straight wire change with current and distance?
cards.back_md: Stronger for **more current**; weaker **further away**.

cards.front_md: Field at the centre of a circular loop
cards.back_md: **Nearly straight** lines perpendicular to the loop; increases with current and **number of turns**.

cards.front_md: Field inside a long solenoid
cards.back_md: **Uniform**: parallel straight lines. Outside: like a **bar magnet**.

cards.front_md: Current seen anticlockwise from one end of a solenoid: which pole?
cards.back_md: **North** pole (clockwise → south).

cards.front_md: Why is soft iron used in an electromagnet?

cards.front_md: Two ways to make an electromagnet stronger
cards.back_md: More **turns**; more **current** (and a soft iron core).

cards.front_md: When is the force on a current in a magnetic field largest, and when zero?
cards.back_md: Largest when **perpendicular** to the field; **zero** when parallel.

cards.front_md: Fleming’s left-hand rule
cards.back_md: Left hand, mutually perpendicular: **First finger Field**, **seCond finger Current**, **thuMb Motion**.

cards.front_md: What happens to the force if both current and field are reversed?
cards.back_md: It stays in the **same direction**.

cards.front_md: Electrons move east in a downward field. Force?
cards.back_md: Current is west; force towards the **south**.

cards.front_md: Two devices that use the force on a current in a field
cards.back_md: **Electric motor**, **loudspeaker**.

cards.front_md: DC vs AC

How often does 50 Hz AC reverse direction?

cards.front_md: One advantage of AC over DC

cards.back_md: **Electromagnetic induction**: a changing magnetic field induces current; mechanical → electrical energy.

questions.stem_md: The direction of the magnetic field at a point is taken as the direction in which

options.text_md: the north pole of a small compass needle points when placed there
the south pole of a compass needle points
iron filings move when the paper is tapped
the magnet would move if released

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: By convention, the field direction at a point is the way the north pole of a compass needle points there.
Step 2: So (a).
Step 3: The south pole (b) points the opposite way. Filings show the shape of the lines, not their direction (c). The magnet’s own motion (d) is not how the field is defined.

questions.stem_md: A thin slot is cut along the axis through the middle of a long bar magnet, and a tiny compass is slid into the slot. In which direction does the north pole of the compass needle point?

options.text_md: Towards the south pole of the magnet
Towards the north pole of the magnet
In no fixed direction, because there is no field inside a magnet
At right angles to the magnet

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Field lines are closed curves: outside the magnet they run from N to S, and inside they continue from S to N.
Step 2: A compass needle points along the field, so inside the magnet its north pole points towards the magnet’s north pole (b).
Step 3: (a) is the direction outside the magnet near its middle; there is a field inside (c is wrong); along the axis the field is not at right angles to the magnet (d).

questions.stem_md: On a field-line drawing of a bar magnet, point X is just beside the N pole, where the lines are crowded, and point Y is far from the magnet, where they are widely spaced. Shalini places the same small compass first at X and then at Y. What will she notice?

options.text_md: The needle is pulled more weakly at X than at Y
The needle points in exactly the same direction at both points
The needle is pulled more strongly at X than at Y
The needle does not respond at X, because the lines are too crowded

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Crowded field lines mean a stronger field; widely spaced lines mean a weaker field.
Step 2: So the magnet acts more strongly on the needle at X than at Y (c).
Step 3: (a) reverses the rule. The field direction usually differs from place to place (b). A strong field makes the needle respond more, not less (d).

questions.stem_md: Why can two magnetic field lines never cross each other?

options.text_md: Because field lines are closed curves
Because field lines repel each other
Because the field is zero where lines meet
Because a compass at the crossing would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: At any point the magnetic field has only one direction, shown by a compass needle.
Step 2: At a crossing there would be two tangents, so two directions at once: impossible. So (d).
Step 3: Being closed curves (a) does not prevent crossing; lines do not "repel" (b); (c) is not true.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Magnetic field lines are closed curves.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Outside a magnet lines run from N to S; inside, from S to N.
Step 2: So every line closes on itself. The statement is true.

questions.stem_md: The region around a magnet in which its force can be detected is called its magnetic ___.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The force of a magnet acts in the space around it.
Step 2: That region is the magnetic field.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet are crowded together near its poles.

**Reason (R):** The relative strength of a magnetic field is shown by how close together the field lines are.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Field lines are indeed crowded near the poles: A is true.
Step 2: The closeness of field lines shows the strength of the field: R is true.
Step 3: The field is strongest near the poles, and R explains why that appears as crowded lines. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Describe how you would trace one magnetic field line of a bar magnet using a small compass, a sheet of paper and a pencil.

answer.model_answer_md: Place the magnet on the paper and draw its outline. Put the compass near the **N pole** and mark the positions of **both ends of the needle** with dots. Move the compass so that its **south end sits on the dot** at its north end, and mark again. Repeat **step by step** until the compass reaches the **S pole**. Joining the dots with a smooth curve gives a field line; arrows from N to S show its direction.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Mark the two ends of the needle.
Step 2: Move the compass forward step by step.
Step 3: Join the dots and add arrows.

marking_scheme.step: Marking the needle ends and moving the compass step by step
Joining the dots into a smooth curve with arrows N to S

questions.stem_md: Two bar magnets are placed on a table with their north poles facing each other a short distance apart. What would iron filings sprinkled between them show?

options.text_md: Field lines from each N pole bending away from each other, with a nearly field-free point midway
Straight field lines joining the two N poles
No pattern at all, because like poles cancel all the field
Field lines crossing each other midway between the poles

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Both poles send field lines outwards; near the middle the two fields oppose each other.
Step 2: The lines turn aside, away from each other, leaving a point midway where the field is nearly zero (a).
Step 3: Lines do not join two N poles (b); the field cancels only at the midpoint, not everywhere (c); field lines never cross (d).

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a magnetic field? How is its direction at a point defined?
(b) State four properties of magnetic field lines.
(c) Describe (in words) the field-line pattern of a bar magnet.
(d) Why do two field lines never intersect?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **region around a magnet** in which its magnetic force can be detected. Its direction at a point is the direction in which the **north pole of a compass needle** points when placed there.

(b) (i) Outside a magnet they go from **N to S**; inside, from S to N, so they are **closed curves**. (ii) The **tangent** at a point gives the field direction. (iii) Lines are **closer** where the field is **stronger**. (iv) **No two lines cross.**

(c) Curved lines leave the N pole, spread out round the sides of the magnet and enter the S pole; they are crowded near the poles and widely spaced far away; the lines along the axis go straight out from N and straight into S.

(d) At a crossing point the field would have **two directions**, so a compass would have to point two ways at once, which is **impossible**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Define the field and its direction.
Step 2: List four properties.
Step 3: Describe the pattern.
Step 4: Explain non-crossing.

questions.stem_md: When Oersted switched on the current in a wire placed just above and along a compass needle, he observed that the needle

options.text_md: did not move
turned away from the direction of the wire
was attracted to the wire and stuck to it
spun round continuously

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The current produced a magnetic field around the wire.
Step 2: The compass needle, originally along the wire, was deflected (turned aside), so (b); reversing the current deflected it the other way.
Step 3: (a), (c) and (d) do not match the observation.

questions.stem_md: Current flows vertically downwards in a straight wire. Seen from above, the magnetic field lines around it are

options.text_md: anticlockwise circles
straight lines pointing downwards
clockwise circles
straight lines radiating outwards from the wire

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Right-hand thumb rule: thumb along the current (downwards).
Step 2: Seen from above, the curled fingers run clockwise, so the field lines are clockwise circles (c).
Step 3: Anticlockwise (a) is for an upward current. The lines are circles, not straight lines (b, d).

questions.stem_md: A compass needle placed 2 cm from a long straight wire carrying a steady current is deflected through 50°. The compass is moved to 10 cm from the wire, the current staying the same. The deflection will

options.text_md: increase, because the field spreads out further
stay at 50°, because the current is the same
reverse, because the compass is now on the far side of the field
decrease, because the wire’s field is weaker further away

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The field of a straight wire becomes weaker with distance from the wire.
Step 2: At 10 cm the wire’s field is weaker compared with the Earth’s field, so the needle is deflected less (d).
Step 3: (a) and (b) ignore the weakening with distance; moving further away on the same side does not reverse the field (c).

questions.stem_md: A horizontal cable carries a current from south to north. A compass is placed directly below the cable. Which way does the north pole of the compass needle swing?

options.text_md: Towards the west
Towards the east
It keeps pointing north
Straight upwards towards the cable

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Right thumb pointing north along the current; the fingers curl round the cable.
Step 2: Below the cable the curled fingers point towards the west, so the field there is westward and the N pole swings west (a).
Step 3: East (b) is the direction above the cable. The needle does turn (c is wrong), and a compass needle turns horizontally, not upwards (d).

questions.stem_md: A circular loop of wire lies flat on a table. Seen from above, the current in it flows anticlockwise. What is the direction of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop?

options.text_md: Horizontal, along the table towards the north
Vertically upwards, out of the table
Vertically downwards, into the table
There is no field at the centre

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Curl the fingers of the right hand along the current (anticlockwise as seen from above); the thumb points upwards.
Step 2: The field at the centre is perpendicular to the loop and points vertically upwards (b).
Step 3: The field at the centre is not along the table (a); downwards (c) is for a clockwise current; the contributions add, so the field is not zero (d).

questions.stem_md: The magnetic field inside a long current-carrying solenoid is

options.text_md: zero
strongest at the ends and zero in the middle
uniform: the same at all points
in the form of concentric circles

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Inside a long solenoid the field lines are parallel straight lines.
Step 2: Parallel, equally spaced lines mean the field is uniform (c).
Step 3: The field is not zero (a), not concentrated at the ends (b), and not circular inside (d).

questions.stem_md: Looking at one end of a current-carrying solenoid, Farhan sees the current in the turns flowing anticlockwise. That end of the solenoid behaves as

options.text_md: a south pole
a neutral point
a south pole, until the current is increased
a north pole

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Curl the right-hand fingers along the current (anticlockwise as seen from that end); the thumb points out towards you.
Step 2: The thumb points to the N pole, so the end facing Farhan is a north pole (d).
Step 3: A clockwise current would make it a south pole (a); the polarity does not depend on the size of the current (c); (b) is wrong.

questions.stem_md: In an electric bell, an electromagnet pulls a soft iron armature (striker) and then releases it, again and again. A repair shop replaces the soft iron core of the electromagnet with a steel core. What is the most likely result?

options.text_md: The striker stays stuck to the core, because steel stays magnetised when the current stops
The bell rings louder, because steel is stronger
Nothing changes, because steel and soft iron behave alike
The bell rings faster, because steel loses its magnetism more quickly

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The bell works only if the core loses its magnetism each time the current is broken, releasing the striker.
Step 2: Steel keeps its magnetism, so the striker stays attracted and the bell does not ring properly (a).
Step 3: (b), (c) and (d) ignore, or reverse, the key difference between steel and soft iron.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil increases when the number of turns is increased.

**Reason (R):** A soft iron core can be placed inside a coil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The fields of the turns add up, so more turns give a stronger field: A is true.
Step 2: A soft iron core can be inserted in a coil: R is true.
Step 3: R does not explain why more turns strengthen the field. So (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The magnetic field lines of a long straight current-carrying wire are straight lines parallel to the wire.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The field lines of a straight wire are concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire.
Step 2: So the statement is false.

questions.stem_md: Coil P has 20 turns and carries 2 A; coil Q has the same radius, 50 turns and carries 1 A. The field at the centre of a coil is proportional to the number of turns multiplied by the current. Find the ratio of the field at the centre of Q to that of P.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: For P: $n I = 20 \times 2 = 40$.
Step 2: For Q: $n I = 50 \times 1 = 50$.
Step 3: Ratio $= \dfrac{50}{40} = 1.25$.
Answer: 1.25 (Q’s field is 1.25 times P’s).

match_right.text_md: Curves from the N pole to the S pole
Nearly straight lines perpendicular to the loop

questions.stem_md: Match each arrangement with the shape of its magnetic field lines.

options.text_md: Long straight wire carrying current
Centre of a circular current loop
Inside a long solenoid
Outside a bar magnet

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Straight wire — concentric circles (p–2).
Step 2: Centre of a loop — nearly straight lines perpendicular to its plane (q–4).
Step 3: Inside a solenoid — parallel lines, uniform field (r–3).
Step 4: Outside a bar magnet — curves from N to S (s–1).

questions.stem_md: State the right-hand thumb rule. A long straight wire lies along a north–south line on a table, with current flowing towards the north. What is the direction of the magnetic field at a point just above the wire?

answer.model_answer_md: **Right-hand thumb rule:** hold the current-carrying wire in the right hand with the **thumb pointing along the current**; the direction in which the **fingers curl** gives the direction of the magnetic field lines. With the thumb pointing north, the fingers curl so that just **above** the wire they point towards the **east**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: State the rule.
Step 2: Apply it: thumb north; above the wire the fingers point east (below, west).

marking_scheme.step: Field above the wire points east

questions.stem_md: Nikhil is building a model crane for a science fair. Its electromagnet must lift a steel toy car and release it when he presses a switch. Describe how he should make the electromagnet, give two ways to make it lift a heavier car, and explain why it should not have a permanent-magnet core.

answer.model_answer_md: He should wind **insulated copper wire** as a **solenoid** round a **soft iron** rod and connect it to a battery through a **switch**; with current flowing, the iron becomes a strong magnet. To lift a heavier car he can (i) **increase the number of turns** and (ii) **increase the current** (more cells). A permanent-magnet core would **stay magnetised when the switch is turned off**, so the car would **not be released**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Construction with a soft iron core and a switch.
Step 2: Two ways to strengthen.
Step 3: Link the need to release the load to temporary magnetism.

marking_scheme.step: Construction: coil on soft iron core with battery and switch
Two ways: more turns, more current
Permanent magnet would not release the car

questions.stem_md: Which change will make an electromagnet stronger?

options.text_md: Removing its soft iron core
Increasing the number of turns of wire
Reversing the direction of the current
Using thicker insulation on the wire

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The fields of the turns add up, so more turns give a stronger field (b).
Step 2: Removing the core (a) weakens it greatly. Reversing the current (c) only swaps the poles. Thicker insulation (d) does not change the field.

questions.stem_md: A solenoid lies horizontally on a bench. Seen from its left end, the current in the turns flows clockwise. Name the poles at its two ends and state the direction of the magnetic field inside it.

answer.model_answer_md: Seen from the **left end** the current is **clockwise**, so the left end is a **south pole**; the **right end is a north pole** (from there the current looks anticlockwise). Inside a solenoid the field runs from S to N, so it points **from left to right**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Clockwise as seen from an end means that end is S.
Step 2: The other end is N; inside, the field runs S to N.

marking_scheme.step: Left end S, right end N
Field inside from left to right

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe the pattern of magnetic field lines around a long straight conductor carrying current. How does the field change if (i) the current is increased, (ii) the distance from the wire is increased?
(b) Describe the field at the centre of a circular loop and explain why a coil of n turns gives a stronger field.
(c) What is a solenoid? Describe its field inside and outside.
(d) How is the polarity of each end of a solenoid found?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Concentric circles** centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it; direction by the **right-hand thumb rule**. (i) Larger current → **stronger** field. (ii) Further away → **weaker** field.

(b) Near the wire the lines are small circles; at the **centre** they are **nearly straight** and perpendicular to the plane of the loop, because every part of the loop produces a field in the **same direction** there. In a coil of n turns the current flows the same way in each turn, so the fields **add up**: about **n times** that of one turn.

(c) A **solenoid** is a coil of many circular turns of insulated wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder. **Inside**, the field lines are parallel straight lines: the field is **uniform**. **Outside**, the pattern is like that of a **bar magnet**, with N and S poles at the ends.

(d) Curl the fingers of the **right hand** in the direction of the current in the turns; the **thumb points to the north pole**. (Equivalently: anticlockwise current seen from an end means that end is N.)

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Straight wire pattern and dependences.
Step 2: Loop and the adding of fields from n turns.
Step 3: Solenoid definition and field.
Step 4: Right-hand rule for polarity.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Field at centre and effect of n turns

questions.stem_md: Aditi placed a compass at different distances from a long vertical wire carrying a steady current and noted how far the needle was deflected from north: 2 cm — 60°, 4 cm — 40°, 8 cm — 22°, 16 cm — 11°. What do these readings show? What would you expect to happen at 4 cm if the current were doubled? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: The deflection **decreases as the distance increases**, so the magnetic field of the wire becomes **weaker further from the wire** (the Earth’s field, which pulls the needle north, stays the same). If the current were doubled, the wire’s field at 4 cm would become **stronger**, so the deflection would be **more than 40°**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Read the trend in the data.
Step 2: Link the deflection to the strength of the wire’s field.
Step 3: Predict the effect of a larger current.

marking_scheme.step: So the field weakens with distance
Doubling current: stronger field, deflection greater than 40°

questions.stem_md: The force on a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field is greatest when the angle between the conductor and the field is
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The force is largest when the current is perpendicular to the field.
Step 2: So at 90° (c).
Step 3: At 0° and 180° (a, d) the conductor is parallel to the field and there is no force; at 45° (b) the force is smaller.

questions.stem_md: In Fleming’s left-hand rule, the thumb points in the direction of the

options.text_md: magnetic field
current
electron flow
force on (motion of) the conductor

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: First finger — field; second finger — current; thumb — motion or force.
Step 2: So (d).
Step 3: The field (a) and current (b) are the fingers; the rule uses conventional current, not electron flow (c).

questions.stem_md: A horizontal rod between the poles of a magnet carries current towards you, while the magnetic field points vertically downwards. In which direction is the rod pushed?

options.text_md: To your right
To your left
Upwards
Away from you

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Left hand: first finger down (field), second finger towards you (current).
Step 2: The thumb points to your right, so the rod is pushed to the right (a).
Step 3: Left (b) would need one of the two reversed. The force cannot be along the field (c) or along the current (d).

questions.stem_md: A beam of electrons travelling towards the east enters a region where the magnetic field points vertically downwards. The beam is deflected towards the

options.text_md: north
south
west
east

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Electrons are negative, so the current is towards the west.
Step 2: Left hand: first finger down, second finger west; the thumb points south (b).
Step 3: North (a) would be the answer for positive charges moving east. The force is perpendicular to the motion, so not east or west (c, d).

questions.stem_md: If both the current in a rod and the magnetic field are reversed, the force on the rod

options.text_md: reverses
becomes zero
stays in the same direction
doubles

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Reversing the current reverses the force; reversing the field reverses it again.
Step 2: Two reversals cancel, so the force stays in the same direction (c).
Step 3: It reverses only if one of them is reversed (a); it does not vanish (b) or double (d).

questions.stem_md: Between the poles of a magnet, a rod carrying current is first placed at right angles to the field, and it is pushed 1 cm sideways. The magnet is then turned slowly until the field lies along the rod. As the magnet turns, the sideways push on the rod

options.text_md: increases steadily
stays the same
reverses direction
decreases and becomes zero when the field lies along the rod

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The force is largest when the current is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel.
Step 2: As the angle between the rod and the field shrinks, the force decreases, reaching zero when they are parallel (d).
Step 3: It does not increase (a) or stay constant (b), and turning the magnet through less than a right angle does not reverse it (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A current-carrying conductor placed perpendicular to a magnetic field experiences a force.

**Reason (R):** The force on such a conductor acts along the direction of the magnetic field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A conductor perpendicular to a field does experience a force (largest in this position): A is true.
Step 2: The force is perpendicular to both the field and the current, not along the field: R is false.
Step 3: So (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Reversing only the direction of the current in a conductor placed in a magnetic field reverses the direction of the force on it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In Fleming’s left-hand rule, turning the second finger round (current) turns the thumb round (force).
Step 2: So the force reverses. The statement is true.

questions.stem_md: The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is given by Fleming’s ___-hand rule.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The right hand is used for the field produced by a current.
Step 2: The force on a current in a field uses Fleming’s left-hand rule.

questions.stem_md: State Fleming’s left-hand rule.

answer.model_answer_md: Stretch the **thumb, first finger and second finger** of the **left hand** so that they are **mutually perpendicular**. If the **first finger** points in the direction of the **magnetic field** and the **second finger** in the direction of the **current**, then the **thumb** points in the direction of the **force (motion)** on the conductor.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Left hand, three mutually perpendicular digits.
Step 2: Assign field, current and force.

marking_scheme.step: Left hand, three digits mutually perpendicular
First finger field, second finger current, thumb force

questions.stem_md: A wire is placed between the poles of a magnet so that the magnetic field points from left to right (→) across the page. Using Fleming’s left-hand rule, find the direction of the force on the wire when the current flows (a) into the page, (b) out of the page, and (c) from left to right along the field.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Current **into the page**, field to the right: the force is **downwards** (towards the bottom of the page).
(b) Current **out of the page**: the force is **upwards**.
(c) Current **parallel to the field**: **no force**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Point the first finger to the right (field).
Step 2: Point the second finger into the page: the thumb points down the page. Reverse the current (out of the page): the thumb points up.
Step 3: Current along the field: no force.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe an activity to show that a current-carrying conductor experiences a force in a magnetic field.
(b) How does the direction of the force change when (i) the current is reversed, (ii) the poles of the magnet are interchanged?
(c) When is the force largest, and when is it zero?
(d) State the rule used to find the direction of the force, and name two devices that use this force.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Suspend a **light aluminium rod** horizontally between the poles of a **horseshoe magnet**, with the field vertical and the rod perpendicular to it. Connect the rod to a battery through a **key** (and a rheostat). On closing the key the rod is **displaced sideways**, showing that a force acts on it.

(b) (i) Reversing the current **reverses** the displacement. (ii) Interchanging the poles also **reverses** it.

(c) **Largest** when the current is **perpendicular** to the field; **zero** when it is **parallel** to the field.

(d) **Fleming’s left-hand rule**: with thumb, first and second fingers of the left hand mutually perpendicular, first finger along the field and second along the current, the thumb gives the force. Devices: **electric motor** (fans, pumps), **loudspeaker**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Describe the rod-and-magnet activity.
